Copper. A soft, malleable, and ductile transition metal that conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well. It has a distinctive reddish-orange metallic lustre and was one of the very first metals humans ever smelted. When alloyed with tin, copper created bronze and sparked the entire Bronze Age of human civilization. Today it remains essential for electrical wiring, plumbing, and countless industrial applications.

Copper has an unusual electron configuration—[Ar] 3d10 4s1—that gives it stability by having a completely filled d-subshell alongside a half-filled s-subshell. When exposed to moist air, it corrodes to form a green patina of basic copper carbonate, a layer that actually protects the metal underneath from further weathering. You'll see this on the Statue of Liberty. Copper alloys readily with other metals to make bronze when combined with tin, and brass when combined with zinc. In biology, hemocyanin is a copper-based protein that turns blue when it binds oxygen; many mollusks and arthropods use this instead of the iron-based hemoglobin found in vertebrates. Copper also functions as a catalyst in click chemistry, particularly in the copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition reaction, which links molecular building blocks together. Gold belongs alongside copper in Group 11, the coinage metals. Iron eventually replaced copper alloys for tools and weapons, marking the historical shift from the Bronze Age. Zinc combines with copper in various ratios to produce brass.
